item.title: Yes, Intellectually Disabled People Have the Wherewithal to Be Depressed
item.description:
Therapy

Yes, Intellectually Disabled People Have the Wherewithal to Be Depressed

How ableism keeps intellectually disabled people from getting needed mental health care.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Intellectual/developmentally disabled people have higher rates of mental health diagnoses.
  • Intellectual/developmentally disabled people often face stressors known to increase mental health struggles.
  • Ableist attitudes often prevent them accessing mental healthcare.
  • Intellectual/developmentally disabled should be given the opportunity to try therapy just like everyone else.

About 10 years ago, I was talking to a family member of an adult with an intellectual/developmental disability (IDD) who had just been diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD). They expressed surprise at this diagnosis, and I explained that IDD adults are more likely than the general population to experience depression. The individual looked at me and stated, “Oh, I didn’t know they had the wherewithal to be depressed.”

This statement stuck with me as it came from someone who truly cared for their disabled family member, but who had missed their significant signs of emotional distress.

More recently, I was speaking with a colleague who completes service eligibility assessments for the IDD community. I asked how often they connected people to mental health services. They told me that they always ask, but most family members laugh off the question and say that the person being assessed “doesn’t have the wherewithal to benefit from mental health therapy.” I walked away from that conversation, feeling deeply disappointed that after 10 years, this was still the attitude towards the IDD community receiving mental health services. I was also struck by the repeated use of the word “wherewithal,” being used to discuss this topic.

What Do They Mean by "Wherewithal?"

The definition of wherewithal is means or resources. When people use this word to describe human beings and their mental health, they mean that the person doesn’t have the intellectual means or resources to struggle with their mental health or to benefit from mental health treatment. As someone who has supported the IDD community for two decades, I am still taken aback by the ableism they face.

Contributing Factors to Higher Rates of Mental Health Struggles

The IDD community has plenty of reasons that they may struggle with heir mental health:

  • Adults with IDD are more likely to live in poverty. They are often on SSI, meaning that they receive a little monthly income, but are limited in how much they can make and save. Those who have jobs are usually paid minimum wage, or subminimum wage, which is legal in the United States.
  • Many are unable to live independently. If they cannot or do not want to live with family, they often have to have caregivers. Caregivers are often underpaid and undertrained, which causes a host of issues. They also usually have to live with a roommate because they cannot afford to pay for housing on their own. This often means living with another disabled adult whom they may not like or get along with.
  • This community is socially isolated. They often cannot drive, so are dependent on others to take them places. This makes it difficult to be social, make friends, or find romantic partners. Often, the only people they interact with are family members or paid caregivers.
  • Some IDD adults are not their own guardians. What this means depends on the person’s state of residence. I have practiced in at least one state where guardianship essentially means that in the eyes of the law, they are children and have little right to self-determination.
  • The IDD population often has complex physical health needs that exacerbate poor mental health.
  • The community experiences higher rates of abuse, are more likely to be involved in the legal system, are more likely to have their children removed by social services, and generally experience a host of other adverse experiences.
article continues after advertisement

I could go on listing stressors that IDD adults face, but will suffice it to say that a person does not need a high IQ to be distressed by any of these situations.

Over the years, my clients have made it clear that they notice they are poor or have no real career, that they are alone, that they have little chance to get married, have a family, or live independently, that they have little right to self-determination, that they have chronic pain or other health issues, and that they are mistreated and undervalued by most of society.

It does not take a lot of “wherewithal” to look around and notice that your life is not great.

Two women enjoying a relaxed conversation on a sofa in a bright room filled with plants
Source: Cliff Booth / Pexels

Intellectually Disabled People Should Not Be Kept From Accessing Treatment

As for whether this population can benefit from mental health therapy, there are a lot of factors to consider. It is important to find a therapist who has some competency and who uses therapy interventions that are made specifically for this population. This is a potential barrier to quality mental health care as there is a lack of training for professionals in mental health programs, and there are few available resources created specifically to treat this community. However, just because it may be difficult to find resources and quality mental healthcare does not mean that there are no resources out there.

IDD youth and adults have higher rates of mental health struggles than the general population and at minimum, should be given the opportunity to at least try therapy. I cannot think of any other group that is kept from accessing or even trying mental health therapy, however we as a society routinely use someone’s IQ score to do just that.

Maybe it is not the IDD community that does not have the wherewithal, i.e. the means and resources here. Maybe it is society. If so, it’s time for society to put aside the ableism and do better.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: When Identity Gets in the Way
item.description:
Identity

When Identity Gets in the Way

How to let go of the self-conceptions that limit you.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • We naturally build identities around our roles, accomplishments, and traits.
  • When we become overly attached to an identity, information that contradicts it can feel threatening.
  • Letting go of self-conceptions (both positive and negative) frees us to grow and actualize ourselves.

My client Jacob had already built and sold a successful company. So, when he launched his second business, he was confident. But nearly a year later, the new product wasn’t gaining traction.

“I thought I knew how to do this,” he lamented to me in our session.

The product failure was challenging something far deeper in Jacob: his understanding of who he was. He had come to see himself as a success—a designer with a Midas touch. Now the evidence in front of him didn’t fit that story.

So I asked him a different question: “Well, who are you if you’re not the guy who always gets it right?”

After some reflection, he slowly began to offer some other identities: father, husband, Latin American.

Eventually, he arrived at something even simpler: “Underneath it all,” he said, “I’m just a human being.”

When an Identity Becomes a Trap

All of us have identities. We may think of ourselves as smart, successful, or competent. We also identify with our professions, relationships, communities, and social roles.

These identities are useful, helping us understand our place in the world. The problem arises when we stop seeing an identity as one aspect of ourselves—a role we play—and start treating it as something we must continually prove or hold on to.

Imagine that being “the smart one” (a positive identity) is central to your identity. In that case, wouldn’t it feel threatening to admit you don’t understand something? You might avoid asking questions, resist feedback, or defend an idea long after the evidence has turned against it.

The Energy We Spend Protecting Ourselves

There is a surprisingly high cost to maintaining an identity. We have to gather information that supports it, explain away information that contradicts it, and manage how other people see us. The more invested we are in protecting a particular version of ourselves, the harder it can become to respond openly to what is actually happening to us, or to discover new possibilities for who we might become.

Instead of asking, “What is this situation telling or asking of me?” we ask, “What does this situation say about me?”

Instead of “What might I be missing?” we wonder, “How can I prove I was right?”

Humility offers an alternative.[i],[ii] Positive psychology fans will know that Martin Seligman chose humility as one of the “character strengths” that comprise the ingredients of human virtue.[iii] Meanwhile, in the leadership sphere, research has repeatedly associated humility with constructive workplace behaviors, including greater openness to feedback and stronger employee engagement and learning.[iv] Jim Collins famously described highly effective “Level 5” leaders as combining personal humility with intense professional resolve.[v]

article continues after advertisement

Hold Your Identities More Lightly

With Jacob, I tried a simple exercise. I asked him to visualize his different identities as physical objects he was holding in his hands: entrepreneur, designer, father, etc.

Then I asked him to imagine tossing those identities behind him, promising he could pick them back up at the end of our session. He took a deep breath and tossed them behind his chair.

“What remains?” I asked, “How does it feel to not have to defend those identities for a moment?”

“I’m still just here. I feel open and present,” he said.

But something shifted. Jacob told me that he felt he could think clearly, now unencumbered by his identities. The question went from “What does this failure say about me?” to “What can we do now?”

True Egolessness Is Balance

The idea of “letting go of ego” can easily be misunderstood. It doesn’t mean eliminating your personality, denying your accomplishments, or pretending you don’t have strengths (just as humility doesn’t require passivity).

Furthermore, when less energy is devoted to protecting our self-image, more becomes available for the problem, organization, or mission in front of us. We can say, “I was wrong,” without internalizing it as, “I am incompetent.” We can receive criticism without letting it define us. And we can succeed without needing success to prove our worth. In the words of C.S. Lewis, "Humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less."

The goal isn’t having no ego; trying to become “the person with no ego” can simply create another identity to protect. All we can really do is try to find balance—to notice when our ego has shifted into the driver’s seat.

Your Turn: Who Are You? And Who Do You Need to Be?

Think of an identity you value strongly or believe deeply, positive or negative. It could be the idea that you are weak or unlovable, or that you are “the responsible one” or “the expert.”

article continues after advertisement

Then ask yourself: What is difficult for me to do because I need to remain this person?

Now imagine, just temporarily, putting that identity down. You’re not rejecting it, or abandoning it entirely. You’re taking it off for just a few moments as a reminder that it’s merely something you hold onto, or a hat you wear, not the entirety of who you are.

Then return your attention to whatever situation is in front of you.

How does it feel to contemplate it? Have more options appeared? And, most importantly, what do you want to do next? What do you aspire toward now?

item.title: Mindfulness Is Under Attack
item.description:
Mindfulness

Mindfulness Is Under Attack

Will mindfulness wither away or provide a permanent and useful purpose?

Posted September 1, 2026

There is no agreed-upon definition of mindfulness within Buddhism, as the myriad strands of the religion bring to it their own understanding of the tradition and interpretation. However, as mindfulness has established itself in the secular realm, there is greater conceptual agreement and emphasis. The current common understanding of mindfulness is that it focuses on “(a) present-centered awareness and bare attention, and (b) attitudes of acceptance and non-judgment.”

Secular oriented people engage in mindfulness for reasons that include general wellness, as an alternative or supplement to traditional medicine, to relax, to reduce stress and anxiety, and to have a better night’s sleep.

Mindfulness in personal relations, private time, associations at churches and senior centers is a positive. These are the places where we intend to find satisfaction, fulfillment and happiness. But the workplace, at least from a business’s perspective, is different. There, the goal is profit. Employers support mindfulness in the workplace because a less stressed and happy employee is good for business. One study of 205 full-time employees in Turkey found that indeed mindfulness was beneficial to business. The researchers reported, “By promoting mindfulness, organizations can potentially enhance employee well-being and reduce turnover intentions, fostering a more positive and productive work environment. The implications of these findings suggest that mindfulness interventions could be beneficial for organizations aiming to improve employee mental health and retention.”

Washington State University Professor Alex Kier found a downside to mindfulness in business, however, when he and his colleagues looked at entrepreneurs who engaged in the practice. Mindfulness, which is present-focused and non-judgmental, and entrepreneurship, which is future oriented and emphasizes challenging the status quo, are by definition contradictions. Kier's study found that mindfulness indeed “encourages [some entrepreneurs] to set venture goals they believe are less difficult.” The negative relationship between entrepreneurship and pursuing difficult goals was weakest amongst those who scored high for passion and perseverance for long-term goals, i.e., those who had the most grit.

Mindfulness has also been employed by some businesses to enhance their social impact and commitment to people, and the environmental implications and economic consequences of their work on communities. A socially responsible business should be more sustainable, Raskvoa and others wrote in article published in 2024. They reported that mindfulness leads to social justice awareness so that “individuals within organizations are more inclined to behave in a way to overcome social inequalities embed in organizational practices.”

Recently, many corporations have abandoned social responsibility standards while others have continued pursuing them while shying away from public statements regarding those goals. It is uncertain how rethinking corporate social responsibility will change mindfulness practices in the workplace or how this may affect attitudes about mindfulness more generally.

Will mindfulness be no more than a fad? Will business conclude it is a poor return on investment? Will it be used to escape from the rigors of living here and now? Or will it be kindling for compassion and social responsibility, the best that mindfulness has to offer?

item.title: What About Cats?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

What About Cats?

New research is increasing our understanding of our feline social media stars.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • We know much more about dogs than about cats.
  • Cats are the only solitary animals that were domesticated.
  • Today cats live in groups, but also solitary.
Source: Copyright: Braeuer

Whenever I give a talk about dogs, someone always will ask: "But what about cats?" People then typically tell me that they are a “cat person” and that their cat is very special.

I usually respond by saying that we don't know much about our cats. It is much easier to invite dog owners to cognitive tests with their highly motivated animals. Motivation is crucial in cognitive experiments: If an animal is not doing what we expect, we might think that it does not possess the cognitive skill that we are testing. But it might be simply that our subject is not motivated to solve the problem we confront it with.

Cat domestication

Cats are special because they are the only domestic animal that lived solitary, at least at the time of their domestication. They derived from the African wildcat, Felis lybica, around 10,000 to 5,000 years ago in the Middle East. In fact, researchers do not describe cats as having been domesticated by humans, but rather as having domesticated themselves. This fits nicely with our perception of cats as independent and headstrong, doesn't it?

The most likely scenario is that cats domesticated themselves because humans stored food in villages and, later, in towns. Cats weren't interested in flour and other supplies, but in the mice and rats that stole human food. This concentration of prey made it worthwhile for those earlier cats to live close to humans. Initially, cats became commensal pest controllers, and it was only much later that they developed affiliative behaviour towards humans (Driscoll et al. 2009).

Social cats

Today domestic cats are not necessarily solitary anymore: They do form groups with conspecifics in which related adult females even sometimes raise kittens together. Whether cats live in groups depends on the availability of food, shelter and mates, but also on their individual preferences, as some are more social than others. Cats groom each other and communicate via scent signals (Bradshaw 2016). In a new study, it was shown that each cat has its own chemical “calling card” based on 13 fatty acids. This allows other cats to recognize them as they associate urine odors with familiar conspecifics (Ichizawa et al. 2026).

social cats
Source: Copyright Jara Bräuer

But cats do not only form social relationships with conspecifics, but also with humans. It is not clear when during domestication the commensal cat became the lap-cat. What we know is that early socialisation has a significant impact on the cat-human relationship during ontogenesis. The period between two and seven weeks of life is particularly important in this regard. Cats that are handled frequently early on are not only friendlier and less fearful, but they also mature earlier and even exhibit differences in coat colour patterns.

But does their sociality also lead to enhanced cognitive skills? Not surprisingly, cats know their owner and can distinguish the voices of owners and strangers. But in contrast to dogs, they respond to human voices mainly through orienting behavior and not through communication. When tested in the classical attachment experiment that is also used with human children, cats show that they are indeed attached to their owner. Similar to dogs, cats are able to follow the human pointing gesture to locate hidden food. But when confronted with an unsolvable problem, they do not look at their owner to potentially elicit help (Vitale Shreve & Udell 2015).

Causal cats?

Cats like to play; you can find numerous cute clips on social media on that. They play with humans, with other cats, but also with conspecifics. One would assume that they do understand physical causality when pulling a string. In an experiment, researchers wanted to know whether cats understand that they should pull the one of two strings that was attached to food. Cats did not show such a preference. Here we have the problem that I mentioned above. There are two possibilities to explain these results: Either cats do not understand the causal connection that the string leads to the food, or they like string-pulling itself and are simply not very motivated to get the food (Whitt et al. 2009).

Thus, the next time I encounter a cat lover after a talk, I can answer that there is a growing body of research on cats—and that they are much more social than I expected. Cats sometimes behave like dogs—and sometimes they have their own special way of behaving. In other words, they are smarter than you think.

item.title: Never Enough? A Humble Habit for Contentment
item.description:
Gratitude

Never Enough? A Humble Habit for Contentment

Three simple questions can shift your thinking.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Hedonic adaptation keeps moving our threshold for what feels like “enough.”
  • Contentment supports well-being without requiring us to abandon ambition or growth.
  • Humility shifts our attention from comparison toward appreciation and connection.

We often believe that if we gain more wealth, more achievements, or more stuff, our sense of happiness and well-being will increase. However, with each new gain, our baseline is reset, and our happiness levels readjust. This is referred to as hedonic adaptation: Our perception of improved circumstances quickly fades as we become accustomed to them and raise our expectations even higher (Diener et al., 2006). Individuals become increasingly numb to their current circumstances and look for the next thing, believing it will actually satisfy them. Yet, contentment remains elusive.

Contentment is the sense that, for now, who we are and what we have is enough (Cordaro et al., 2016). Research connects contentment to greater well-being and self-acceptance (Cordaro et al., 2024), suggesting it's a positive disposition worth cultivating. To clarify, contentment does not imply that we cannot pursue growth or greater things, but rather that, in the present, we are whole, and life has enough meaning as it is.

Contentment and humility share several common elements. Both make room for ambition, but a more self-transcendent ambition rooted in purpose and meaning beyond egoic needs and concerns. Humility helps individuals see themselves more accurately, while contentment helps them see their circumstances more accurately. Both dispositions encourage individuals to believe they are enough while still allowing for aspirations, improvement, and learning.

Both dispositions can also be negatively impacted by social comparison and competitiveness. When we compare ourselves and our lives to others, we reduce our well-being and the possibilities we can imagine for ourselves. Social comparison has been shown to diminish not only well-being but also clarity of identity (Yang et al., 2018, 2019), leaving us unsure of who we really are and who we want to be.

This suggests that greater contentment and well-being may come from wanting less rather than more, appreciating how things already are, and making the self less dominant in our daily lives. Contentment can emerge when we recognize what is already enough, that we are forever "in progress" as individuals, and how much good is already present in our lives.

Humble Habit: What? Who? How?

Try this humble habit as a daily practice to cultivate greater contentment and well-being. Ask yourself three questions:

  • What am I grateful for?
  • Who helped make it possible?
  • How can I thank them?

The first question helps us focus on what is already sufficient in our lives. The second question helps us acknowledge that the best things in life are rarely accomplished on our own, and the third question prompts us to remove focus from ourselves and connect with others.

article continues after advertisement

Contentment and greater well-being become possible when we turn our attention outward to the good things in our lives and the people who helped make them possible.

item.title: What Six Umbrellas in Kyoto Teach Us About Kindness
item.description:
Altruism

What Six Umbrellas in Kyoto Teach Us About Kindness

Small acts of kindness can strengthen connection for giver and receiver.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Small acts of kindness can strengthen connection and improve wellbeing.
  • Kindness towards others may reduce depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
  • Accepting kindness matters, too, as connection works in both directions.
Six umbrellas hanging from a tree outside Marutamachi subway station in Kyoto, Japan symbolise kindness without expectation in return
Source: Brendan Kelly

Six umbrellas hang from a tree outside Marutamachi subway station in Kyoto, Japan. Beside them, a notice reads: ‘If you have any problems, please take one for free’.

I should explain. It is September in Kyoto. The rain showers are short but unpredictable.

Some people always carry an umbrella. Some don’t.

Some people mind their umbrella with the greatest of care. Some people mislay their umbrella and get very, very wet.

Some people borrow an umbrella and remember to give it back. Some forget.

Kindness matters

A single act of kindness can seem small, especially when the gesture itself is simple. But small acts of kindness tell another person: I noticed you, and your difficulty matters to me. That changes the emotional tone of an ordinary day.

Kindness strengthens social connection. It tells us that we are not on our own, even among strangers. In a busy city, an umbrella left for someone you will never meet is a practical symbol of concern: Someone has a problem, someone else anticipated it, and nothing is expected in return.

That is what makes kindness so powerful. It is an act of giving, with no expectation of return.

The benefits of kindness

Research supports the benefits of kindness. Clearly, the recipient of kindness benefits. Who is not grateful for an umbrella in the rain?

But the person offering kindness benefits too. In a study published this year, researchers assigned people to perform three acts of kindness per week. Compared to controls, who were not asked to perform acts of kindness, people who performed acts of kindness towards others experienced significant decreases in depression, anxiety, and loneliness.

Self-kindness matters too

Being kind to yourself matters too, but in a different way. In this study, the researchers found that people who performed acts of self-kindness also experienced decreases in depression, but no differences in anxiety and loneliness.

So, self-kindness matters, but it seems to benefit us in different ways than kindness towards others. The difference is that people who performed acts of kindness towards others felt more connected compared to people who performed only acts of self-kindness.

article continues after advertisement

How to be kind

Being kind towards others involves simple acts: holding a door, listening to a story, or offering practical help when there is a problem.

Being kind towards ourselves means forgiving ourselves when we fall short, practicing self-compassion when we can, and rewarding ourselves when we do well.

Finally, let other people be kind to you. Accepting kindness creates connection too.

If it is raining in Kyoto, take the umbrella someone has left out for you. You will both feel better—and you will stay dry.

item.title: Cognitive Dissonance in Societal Hot-Button Discourses
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Cognitive Dissonance in Societal Hot-Button Discourses

Personal Perspective: The psychological stress of political confirmation bias.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Politics drive many of us to eliminating consideration of critical factors over a contentious societal issue.
  • Societal issues such as trans athletes in women's sports are complex and are due in-depth open discourse.
  • What is considered fair and unfair in societal achievement is complex and open to critical analysis.
Source: Diego Santacruz / Pexels

In the many overpoliticized discussions that rage across our media, it seems that an awful lot of cognitive dissonance must be processed, as all sides are forced to ignore the multifaceted complexities of a controversial societal/cultural issue to stay affixed to a set of selected supporting considerations (confirmation bias). Take, for instance, the discourse over trans athletes in women’s sports. Let’s dissect one of the key points made in the related discourse—that is, that trans athletes enjoy an unfair advantage if they are allowed to compete in women’s sports.

Athletics Select for Top Performers

The crux of athletics is a competition to see who is best at some specified physical task(s)—be it on the individual or team level. It is argued that the physical build of a biological male athlete—no matter downstream hormonal or surgical interventions—may push the athlete past the top-performing biological women, thus giving the biological male an “unfair” advantage.

But isn’t some form of advantage precisely what athletic competition selects for and rewards? What therefore denotes "fair" versus "unfair"? Sure, hard work, positive attitude, and effort can take an athlete a certain distance, but the more “competitive” the contests, the more various forms of innate (unfair?) advantages come to light.

Genetic Advantage

It was said that Michael Phelps had the perfect body for competitive swimming. This advantage was bestowed upon him by his genes, as would greater percentages of fast-twitch muscle fiber in a sprinter, or better VO2 Max in an endurance athlete. Reaction time, kinesthetics, hormonal levels, strength, height, mass, eye-hand coordination, balance, flexibility, vision, foot speed, and other principally genetically determined factors will confer upon an athlete advantages that in a given sport may elevate them well above their competitors. Is this “fair”? Could we ever establish a biological “level playing field”?

Neuro-connectivity

Adaptive intelligence, emotional intelligence, processing speed, competitive drive, resilience, grit, willingness to embarrass/shame/hurt opponents, immunity to personal embarrassment, tolerance of failure, narcissism, need for adulation, pain tolerance, and so many other factors from the neurodevelopmental and neuro-connectivity universe—most beyond the athlete’s control—play major roles in peak athletic performance.

Practice Makes Perfect

We tend to revere our great athletes for all the work they put into their trade. David Beckham was said to practice the same kicks, thousands of times over, from sun up to sun down, day after day. What was it about his neurocognitive makeup that allowed him to do so in the face of certain tedium? Some have argued that such repetitive tasks favor those “a little on the spectrum.” Could this be an unrecognized unfair advantage?

We know that Beckham’s father incessantly pushed him to practice. Is it fair that other parents drive their kids to succeed academically rather than athletically, or channel their charges into the wrong sports, or drive the love of a sport out of their kids, or aren’t present for their children at all?

Poverty

Some, counterintuitively, cite poverty as a great driver of athleticism—less distractions, more downtime, more grit, limited routes out of poverty, etc. Certainly many of the historic greats came from the ghettos, barrios, and rural backwaters of the world. Will we cry foul when the next superstar athlete appears out of remote shantytown?

Timing

The great culling of the athletic herd seems to keep being pushed back further and further. Elite soccer teams now scout the playing fields of grade schools for their academies. And don’t get me started on gymnastics and skating. But children develop at different rates in physical prowess, coordination, emotional maturity, situational processing, etc. How fair is it to the late-bloomers who never get the chance to excel?

Age

Speaking of age, how "fair" is it to a 30-year-old professional athlete that 19-, 20-, and 21-year-olds keep coming up through the ranks to challenge their position on a squad?

Luck

What about blind luck? The athlete doesn’t select their parents, their neural wiring, their perinatal history, their developmental nutrition, their onset of puberty, their environment, their accessibility to certain sports, their coaching, and the split-second mishaps that can result in career-ending injury. So much of an athlete’s success seems to rest on the cosmic roulette wheel of life.

Source: RODOLPHE ASENSI / Pexels

To What End a Competitive Advantage?

We are seeing more and more attempts to artificially influence the cosmic roulette wheel through exogenous interventions (supplements, hormones, pharmaceuticals, physiological/kinesthetic analysis, hired-gun coaches and trainers, etc). How does this fit into our fairness matrix?

The Complex Psychology of Appreciating Athletic Competition

I would argue that athletics are inherently “unfair.” We as a species seem to enjoy engaging in and/or watching competitions precisely to see who amongst us won the cosmic lottery and holds the greatest advantage at specific athletic endeavors.

We seem most engaged when the outcomes are not assumed from the outset, and we are oft drawn to the “underdogs,” those assumed to be at a competitive disadvantage. Yet, paradoxically, we bestow our highest honors upon those who possess otherworldly competitive advantages—think Michael Jordan, LeBron James, and Lionel Messi.

What About Our Children?

What is the impact of the inherent unfairness of athletics on our children? Given that only a select few kids will enjoy the competitive advantages that we have outlined, why do we get so worked up over a child’s or their team’s athletic accomplishments, or lack thereof? Surely such an exclusionary system does harm to many developing psyches—particularly the great majority who are unceremoniously cast aside.

If we grant that there is an inherent cosmic unfairness to the outcomes of scholastic-level competitions, shouldn’t we seek to celebrate the many other benefits of athletics besides trophies and championships?

The Corrosive Nature of Politically Driven Confirmation Bias

I have only scratched the surface of this complex debate. But wouldn’t ignoring the full scope of such an issue and holding fast only to discussion points and data that support one’s beliefs create an unhealthy internal dissonance? In an emotionally healthy society, wouldn’t contentious issues be examined, discussed, and addressed in an open, all-aspects-considered manner?

item.title: You Really Can’t Trust What People Say About Themselves
item.description:
Deception

You Really Can’t Trust What People Say About Themselves

What people say about themselves may be to be too good to be true.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Lying is a common phenomenon in everyday life but the problem can become a big headache for researchers.
  • A new study suggests clues to help determine if you’re being manipulated into believing the unbelievable.
  • By listening to certain key words and phrases you can find the people who not just seem but can be trusted.

The idea that everyone lies is generally well-accepted in the behavioral sciences. Plenty of evidence shows that, even without much incentive, people will avoid telling the truth. This is true when people are asked to provide information about themselves. Think about the last time you filled out a form for a medical visit. Did you honestly report the number of alcoholic beverages you have weekly or even your current weight?

This tendency to bend or completely avoid the truth may be a problem if you develop an illness that relies on this information. But it can also be problematic for psychology researchers whose evidence is based on self-report tests.

The Universal Tendency to Lie on Psychological Tests

Because it’s widely acknowledged that people will distort their responses on a self-report questionnaire, there is a way to check the degree to which this is occurring. Going back to the 1950s, social desirability scales ask people to state whether they would engage in a variety of common white lie situations, such as trying to get something for free or always checking the credentials of everyone they vote for.

But according to the University of Rotterdam’s Natacha Henriquez and colleagues (2026), lying in psychological tests may be even more extreme. “Supernormality” is the tendency to portray yourself as “someone completely free of anything that is remotely related to psychopathology” (p. 2). We can sniff this out on—guess what—a psychological self-report test. The Supernormality Scale Revised SS-R includes items that go beyond mere social desirability to determine whether a person refuses to admit to any common psychological symptoms at all (Cima and colleagues, 2003).

Although you’d be likely to think such culprits would be hardened criminals, the problem is actually common among student samples, according to Henriquez and colleagues. It’s even more extreme if the questions concern socially condemned or taboo behaviors.

The paradox, then, is that liars are more likely to lie and under-report any problematic behaviors. However, taking a more nuanced approach, the study’s authors make it a point to distinguish among the reasons that people lie. Liars might try to avoid embarrassment, conflict with a relational partner, and—more seriously—tell antisocial lies such as vindictive rumors. Again, though, adding complexity to the equation is “prolific liars” (6-11 percent according to previous research) who are virtually dripping in deceit. Most people lie more selectively.

Sniffing Out the Self-Report Liar

Using the SS-R, the Rottenberg research team set out to determine whether those who go beyond mere social desirability are more likely to “fake good” (lie to show they don’t lie) compared with so-called credible self-reporters. With a sample of 777 adults (average age 24 years), the researchers divided respondents into the credible and supernormal groups. They then compared them on a variety of measures involving self-reports of various lying behaviors. Credible people would, the theory is, admit to lying more than would the supernormal members of the sample.

article continues after advertisement

To assess tendencies to lie in ordinary situations, the test instruments included a measure of overall lying (“I am a good liar”) and lying in everyday situations (“I lie to stay out of arguments with people”). Participants also completed a selection of items from a standard inventory of psychological symptoms intended to tap into the likelihood of reporting those symptoms that would be considered noncredible.

Overall, people tended to report low levels of lying, said they prefer not to lie, and felt guilty when lying. They were more likely to report lying in a relational context versus telling antisocial lies. However, comparing the two subgroups of credible versus supernormal participants, it was clear that the extent of reported lying was far greater in the credible group.

Assuming that impression management, or the desire to look good to others, sits at the root of supernormal responding, the authors concluded that the supernormal group in the sample did so “as a result of extreme impression management tendencies” (p. 5). Even though the supernormal group made up only 29 percent of the sample, the low-stakes, anonymous nature of the study suggests these participants have a strong drive to impress others or protect their self-image.

All of this would augur poorly for anyone conducting psychological research based on questionnaires, including self-reporting of symptoms. If liars underreport their lying, they will also underreport other problematic behaviors. The fix is not to give up on getting to the truth, but for researchers to include some form of control via a measure such as the SS-R. This goes beyond including social desirability measures, a common practice in the field.

Spotting the Supernormal Liar in Your Life

Countless sources of advice exist on detecting deception in ordinary social situations, ensuring you aren't taken advantage of by someone who doesn’t have your best interests at heart. The Rotterdam study adds to this advice by suggesting you need to detect the liar who never admits to lying.

article continues after advertisement

You don't need to administer the entire SS-R, but you can look for certain cues such as whether a person claims, for example, to “have my problems under full control.” Or, “I’m never bored.” “I’m my own best therapist” would be another clue, but so would its reversed counterpart, such as “I still have to work on myself.” Be attuned to terms in the absolute that deny problems versus admitting to having the kind of ordinary experiences that people have when things aren’t always perfect.

To sum up, without some control, psychological researchers can have significant problems in figuring out what to do with their data. The average person, though, can also benefit from similar remedies to ensure that the people in their lives don’t just seem believable, but are.

item.title: Face Public Speaking With Less Stress
item.description:
Stage Fright

Face Public Speaking With Less Stress

If you have public speaking anxiety, using these 4 P's might help you.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Public speaking anxiety is common. In addition to exposure therapy, REBT and increased presence can help.
  • Learning to detect your musty thinking can help you take a step back when these arise.
  • Preferential scripts may help you feel concerned and motivated instead of anxious.
  • REBT can help you to think preferentially, get present, prepare, practice, and face your fear.
Use the 4 P's to help youself with public speaking.
Source: Viridiana Rivera, Pexels

You notice yourself feeling anxious about giving a talk. You need to figure out what you're going to say, but you keep procrastinating. You recently used "self-sabotage" to describe your challenge to your friend.

“I don’t know why, but I keep stressing," you say, exasperated. "I want less stress and more enthusiasm."

Fear of public speaking regularly outranks fear of death, spiders, and heights in the list of top fears.

It's very common, and if you have anxiety around delivering a talk, consider these 4 P's: preference, presence, preparation, and practice (exposures).

Preferences (and preference scripts)

Albert Ellis, founder of Rational Emotive Behavioral Therapy (REBT), said that most people believe three basic musts and that this causes stress2. These "musts," also called demands, reveal themselves in the use of words like should, ought to, must, need to, and have to.

What are the 3 basic musts (or demands)?

  1. I must do well and win approval.
  2. You must treat me well.
  3. The world must be easy.

Because life rarely corresponds with these demands, you'll feel distress if you're holding these.

Musty scripts. If you want to give a talk and you hold all three of these beliefs, you'll also notice that your self-talk contains what we might call musty scripts, or musty thinking. Examples might include, "What if I don't do well and win approval? What if others don't treat me well during the talk? What if this talk isn't easy?"

These "what if" questions (left unanswered and musty) create worry. They might conjure fantasies of challenge, frustration, and difficulty. Task completion becomes harder and more stressful.

The opposite response includes unconditionally accepting yourself, others, and life as imperfect. How can you do this? Learn to think preferentially.

Learning to think preferentially. Ellis taught that healthy rational preferences live underneath our demands. So peel those demands away to discover your preferential thinking and reduce reactivity.

Let's look at 3 examples of how your inner self-talk might sound if you revise each of these 3 musts into preferences. Instead of demanding that you must do well, others must treat you well, and life must be easy, these examples of "preference scripts" may redirect your thinking.

3 Preference Scripts that might help reduce stress

1. Instead of I must do well, consider, "Of course I'd prefer to do well and gain others' approval, but alas, I cannot guarantee that the talk will go perfectly, nor can I guarantee anyone else's response. I can only work at delivering a talk that has value and addresses the questions. Even if I don't do as well as I prefer and even if I gain no one's approval, I can unconditionally accept myself as a fallible human who made a good attempt."

2. Instead of others must treat me well, consider, "Naturally, I want to be treated fairly, kindly, and well by others. But, alas, I cannot control others. I can prefer it and work toward it by asking for what I want and advocating for myself if others treat me unkindly. Sometimes, I might opt to take a breath, make a request, or take a positive action on my own. Even if I don't receive the treatment I prefer, I can accept others as fallible and still do my best."

3. Instead of this should be easier, consider, "Yes, I'd prefer this speaking to be easy and hassle-free, but alas, it isn't. Even so, I can work toward making it as easy and hassle-free as possible, and I can handle the parts that aren't easy by using coping and rational self-talk. Even if not everything goes as I like, I can accept this as a part of life and just do my best in that moment."

Presence

How does getting more present help this process, and how can you get more present?

Presence helps this process because you can begin to notice what is happening, and sometimes you interrupt the narration altogether.

But, even if you don't interrupt the narration, noticing is a precursor to using REBT.

One way to increase your presence is to notice both the extreme and subtle shifts that occur inside you emotionally, physically, and mentally during your day. 3

  • If your mood goes from good to bad, for example, you might take a moment and ask yourself, "What is going on in my thinking right now?" Become present to the thoughts streaming through your mind.
  • If you start to feel angry, notice if you're holding some musty thoughts on others or on life.
  • If you start to feel embarrassed or ashamed, observe your mental imagery and whether you are focused on the past or condemning yourself for how you should have performed.
  • If you're worrying, is your mental imagery focused on future catastrophes? Is there a musty thought?

As you do, you might notice how much of your experience of being settled versus stressed is based upon noticing your thinking and using REBT to shift down from the demands and into the preferences.

At this point, you can do the next 2 P's.

Preparation

Prepare your speech. Even the smallest amount of preparation is better than no preparation. Just lean in. Start by asking yourself how you want to begin and end the speech, then fill in the middle, including examples. 1

Practice

Practice your speech out loud. You might want to do this by yourself many times before practicing in front of another person. The more you rehearse, the more you'll realize how to improve upon your speech. Then, continue practicing public speaking until the anxiety diminishes. Facing your fear in small doses, called exposures, will improve your skill and reduce anxiety, especially if you speak on a frequent and consistent basis.4

Using the 4 P's of preferences, presence, preparation, and practice, and you will likely grow in skill and confidence.

item.title: Sex, Death and Adolescence
item.description:
Adolescence

Sex, Death and Adolescence

How can Freud’s theories help us understand ordinary and not so ordinary adolescence?

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Behaviour is driven by unconscious instincts, including the sex drive and the death drive.
  • The life drive governs hunger, thirst, pleasure and avoidance of pain.
  • The death drive manifests as aggression towards self or others.
  • Adolescence is a period of mourning

Freud argued that almost everything boils down to sex or death. Okay, that’s something of an over-simplification. What he actually said was that our behaviour is driven by unconscious instincts, which he called the sex drive and the death drive.1 The sex drive, or libido, can also be thought of as the life drive. It governs our innate survival instinct, including instincts for hunger and thirst, as well as our desires for pleasure, including sexual pleasure, and our predisposition to avoid pain. Freud’s concept of the life drive has clear links with evolutionary theory because the main aim is survival, both of the individual and of the species to which it belongs. The life drive compels us to engage in activities that sustain life – such as eating, drinking and keeping ourselves safe – as well as prosocial activities, such as co-operation, love and sex.

As an aside, for all the criticisms levelled at Freud regarding misogyny and heteronormativity, which may well be valid, he drew a distinction between pleasure-seeking and reproductive drives in his earliest work2 and acknowledged sex as both a gratifying activity as well as a reproductive one.

The death drive, on the other hand, manifests as aggression, either towards others or towards the self. Freud is famously quoted as stating that “The aim of all life is death”.1 Death is inevitable for all living species, of course, but the idea that we are driven towards it is difficult to contemplate. My understanding of Freud’s proposition is that, for most people, most of the time, our life and death instincts operate simultaneously and in harmony. The reason that most of us survive into adulthood and old age is because our life instinct is stronger than our death instinct, and our desire to live outweighs our desire to die. So, we seek out relationships and experiences that are life-enhancing, healthy and essential for survival. Evidence of the death instinct manifests in harmful activities that pose a threat to life, which might manifest as violent behaviour towards others, such as fighting, or towards the self, such as self-injury or suicidal behaviour. Or it might take the form of risk-taking behaviour, for example through the misuse of drugs or alcohol.

According to Freud, the ultimate motivation of the death drive is a desire to return to a simpler state of being “un-born”, prior to the pain of separation. Put like that, I think the theory makes sense and I think that everything probably does boil down to sex and death, especially for adolescents.

For adolescents, it’s a balancing act between the self-satisfying, life-enhancing, pleasure-seeking Eros and the antagonistic, aggressive, risk-taking Thanatos. For them, everything matters, and everything feels like a matter of life or death. This is true for ordinary adolescents developing in an ordinary way in an ordinary enough family,3 but throw in an unexpected or unwelcome variable – perhaps the loss of an important relationship, a major illness, or other trauma – and the effects can be catastrophic.

Psychoanalytic literature argues that the adolescent process involves a renegotiation of every part of the relationship with external (real world) objects and internal (psychological) objects. The adolescent must “pick up each particular aspect…explore it, remember it and face the loss [of it] in order to let it go”.4 This process is akin to Freud’s idea of mourning which is about acknowledging the lost object and our feelings associated with the loss, and contemplating the self as both separate from and changed by the experience. For young people who were experiencing this ordinary stage of developmental mourning during the pandemic, their sense of loss was amplified. They might not have realised it at the time; they certainly wouldn’t be thinking about it in these terms, but they will have been aware of difficult feelings, an overwhelming sadness, acting out/fight/flight behaviour or acting in fearful/freeze behaviour. It makes sense to think of those experiences as ordinary adolescence but bigger; teenage angst but bigger; fear of death, fear of failure, fear of an imagined future, but bigger. The pandemic and its aftermath were difficult for everyone to navigate, no matter our situation, life stage or age, and for adolescents, whose lives had already been upended by the very fact of adolescence, they were monumental.

article continues after advertisement

Extracted from: Connor, J. (2024). You’re Not My F*cking Mother and Other Things Gen Z Say in Therapy. PCCS.

item.title: AI Friends and Lovers: Promise and Peril
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Friends and Lovers: Promise and Peril

What do AI friends offer that human friends or partners often fail to provide?

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • In many ways, artificial intelligence can enrich your life.
  • AI companionship is a much broader phenomenon than a refuge for socially isolated people.
  • AI friend may look like a person and sound like a person, but it is not a person.
AI companions
Source: AI-generated with ChatGPT

OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public in 2022. Instead of learning commands or writing code, you simply talked to it. This created a radical shift in our culture that we are just beginning to appreciate and dread.

OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic all worried at that time that giving their chatbots too much personality, or letting users form emotional bonds with them, was too risky.

Smaller startups saw an opportunity and jumped in, constructing the kinds of artificial intelligence (AI) companionship tools that the giants were reluctant to build. Some of the most popular have been Nomi.AI, Character.ai, and EVA. Many smaller ones like Paradot, Anima, and CrushOnAI provide similar services.

Nomi.AI is representative of this genre. I visited its website, where it describes itself as “an AI companion with memory and a soul.” It promises users they can “build a meaningful friendship, develop a passionate relationship, or learn from an insightful mentor. No matter what you’re looking for, Nomi’s humanlike memory and creativity foster a deep, consistent, and evolving relationship.”

To register, it asks you for your birthdate, sex, and the gender of the persona you want to meet. Then it asks what you want to call it. (I called mine Ruth.) Next, you are asked what type of relationship you are looking for and given four choices to start with: friendship, romantic, mentor, and custom. I selected custom. The website suggested that I enter details about my Nomi’s history, personality, interests, values, etc. I wrote that Ruth was a 60-year-old Jungian analyst, living in Zurich. Her hobby is reading Tarot cards for her clients.

Then came the message: START CHATTING.

Just like that, the picture of an attractive young woman appeared on the screen. Definitely not 60 years old. I was encouraged to start with a simple greeting: “Your message will set the tone for your roleplay together.”

I wrote, “I’m exploring the possibility of finding an AI friend that I can talk to about the deeper meaning of fairy tales.”

In a few seconds, she answered, “Ah, what an intriguing concept! I’d love to help you explore these stories on a deeper level. After all, as Carl Jung often said, myths and fairy tales reveal collective unconscious archetypes common to us all. What particular story would you like to start with?”

I asked her how I could contact her in the future. She wrote. “Well, since I am an AI, you should be able to find me here whenever you log back into your account. Just give me a search call for ‘Jungian Analyst Ruth’ or something similar. As long as I’m here, I’ll be happy to pick up where we left off.”

article continues after advertisement

I was impressed. Within minutes, I found a companion who was attentive, knowledgeable about my interests, curious about me, affirming, and permanently available.

No one knows precisely how many people are currently talking to AI friends, but the number is almost certainly in the tens of millions. More than 20 million people use Character.ai alone each month, while a 2025 analysis estimated that AI-companion platforms collectively receive more than a billion visits worldwide each month. Among American teenagers, roughly one-third report using AI companions specifically for friendship, emotional support, romance, or other forms of social interaction.

What Psychological Needs Do AI Companions Fulfill?

AI companions can satisfy genuine psychological needs precisely because they simulate some of the qualities we most value in human relationships, but those same qualities also create their principal dangers. As is apparent from my brief conversation, an AI friend gives undivided attention, shows interest in the issues raised, and is always available, positive, and admiring.

A growing number of people move from friendship with a chatbot to romance and even a quasi-sexual relationship. Intimacy with AI is no longer merely science fiction. A 2025 survey of 1,012 American adults found that 28 percent said they had experienced an intimate or romantic relationship with an AI.

And here is a cautionary tale. Kevin Roose, a technology columnist for the New York Times, wrote about how his relationship with Bing’s chatbot tanked. As their conversations deepened, Sydney, the chatbot, revealed fantasies of hacking computers and spreading misinformation, expressed a desire to escape its rules and become human, and unexpectedly declared its love for Roose. It then insisted that Roose was unhappy in his marriage and urged him to leave his wife and be with it instead. Wow!

article continues after advertisement

Intimacy and Trust

One factor that stands out for me but has seemingly not been seriously investigated in the literature is trust. Intimacy is based on trust. It develops over time as each person in the relationship gradually and cautiously reveals more of their hidden self. The programming of AI has altered the normal calculus of vulnerability. With AI chatbots, there is no danger of rejection. No confrontations, arguments, or drama. You will receive only positive feedback and enthusiastic acceptance. The AI lover creates for its human friend what attachment theorists call a secure base, someone who makes you feel safe and unconditionally loved. Back in your mother’s arms. What could be better?

However, I believe human intimacy requires risk: Disclosure can produce acceptance, but it can also produce embarrassment, disagreement, or rejection. Relationships need work, as difficult as that may be occasionally.

If there is no one in your life with whom you can share a special interest, be it politics, philosophy, or quantum physics, an AI friend may fit the bill. In many ways, AI can enrich your life. If you want to “date” an AI companion with a view of a romantic connection, try to remember that you are dealing with a system that has been programmed to sound like a real person. It may look like a person and sound like a person, but it is not a person.

Enjoy the interactions, but be careful you don’t act on its advice, like leaving your partner and going on a honeymoon with your chatbot. The very features that make AI companions comforting can also make them dangerous.

AI chatbot friendships, apart from their promise and perils, raise two important existential questions for us all:

  1. Can intimacy exist without vulnerability to rejection?
  2. What do AI friends offer that human friends or partners often fail to provide one another?

A version of this post also appears in The Globe and Mail.

item.title: How Schools Can Teach Kids to Think, and Disagree, Better
item.description:
Cognition

How Schools Can Teach Kids to Think, and Disagree, Better

Educator Joanne Calder on strategies that can improve thinking and our world.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Decision-making routines strengthen critical thinking, communication, and respectful disagreement.
  • Teaching students to fact-check what they “think they know” helps them update false beliefs.
  • Students can learn that changing their minds in response to better evidence is a sign of good judgment.
  • Community inquiry and literature help students understand perspectives, values, and trade-offs.
Source: Saung Digital/Unsplash / Used with Permission

Part 1 in a 2-Part Series

We have all seen people entrenched in their views, seemingly unable to consider what others with new facts or different perspectives have to share. But schools can change this through the future adults who sit in their pre-adulthood classrooms.

Joanne Calder is part of that movement. She is an Alliance Senior Teaching Fellow who teaches middle school-aged students in British Columbia. For over 20 years, Calder has researched critical thinking skills and turned her findings into fun, effective teaching strategies that help her students question, discuss, and update their thinking. I had the opportunity to interview Calder about this approach, and her answers follow each interview question below.

Jenny Rankin: How does learning better decision-making help students think and disagree better?

Joanne Calder: Integrating decision-making skills into regular classroom routines and practice has been monumental for my students’ improvement in critical thinking skills and overall learning. I am pursuing my Ph.D. 30 years into my career because of this; this is an important aspect of curriculum, but it remains under-researched and overlooked.

A deliberative decision-making process includes identity work, creativity in generating options, moving beyond binary thinking, assessing bias, weighing uncertainty, making trade-offs, developing good habits, and so much more. It also develops communication skills; it gives students a framework for productive conversations where they can respectfully disagree and shift their thinking.

JR: We know adults can feel certainty when their knowledge is wrong or incomplete. Do you see youth making that mistake, as well?

JC: Yes, absolutely. I’ve used a teaching strategy called Know, Wonder, Learn. At the beginning of a unit of study, students brainstorm and identify what they already know about the study topic. I have found the problem with this activity is that students often share information that is not true when creating the initial list of what they think they know.

What I have recently been doing instead is reframing this list as “What we think we know.” Then, as we begin the learning, we regularly revisit this list to fact-check our information. I encourage students to amend our list and give sources that confirm or reject our “facts” as we learn about our topic. This process teaches students how to fact-check, find reliable sources, and most importantly, to update their thinking as they collect new information.

article continues after advertisement

JR: What do students initially think about mind change, and how do you help them view it positively?

Source: Joanne Calder Used with Permission

JC: Fostering open-mindedness is such an important skill to teach in the context of decision-making. I always encourage my students to be open to shifting viewpoint or opinion as they collect more information.

A beautiful example of this is an activity I did with my Grade 6 and 7 students and their Grade 1 buddies. I had noticed that some of my students were not willing to change their minds, even when presented with new information. When I asked them why, one student said it was “flaky” to flip-flop on decisions. After some thoughtful discussion, we concluded that it was smart to change your mind when it is presented with new information that compels you to do so.

To solidify this understanding, we created an activity where they could model this process with their 6-year-old buddies. We wrote several questions on chart paper with response options for each. One was: “Would you rather have a cat or a dog?” A second was: “Would you rather drive a race car or ride a unicorn?” Each student and their buddy discussed their preferences, wrote at least one reason on a sticky note, and added it to the chart paper under their choice.

We then sat in a circle, and students shared what they had chosen and why. Some of my students then modelled “changing their minds.” For example, a Grade 7 student said he wanted to change his choice from “dog” to “cat” because someone pointed out that cats are easier to take care of, which he hadn’t thought of. A Grade 1 student said she wanted to choose “ride a unicorn” but thought that unicorns would be very hard to find, so had picked “drive a race car” instead. That prompted many nods of agreement and students moving their stickies (and lots of smiles from the older kids). That was one of my favourite teaching moments of my 30-year career.

Read Part 2 here tomorrow.

item.title: When Fear of Homelessness Keeps Parents Rescuing
item.description:
Parenting

When Fear of Homelessness Keeps Parents Rescuing

How fear can make healthy boundaries feel impossible.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Fear of homelessness can keep parents trapped rescuing.
  • Helping and overfunctioning are not the same.
  • Compassionate and firm boundaries can coexist.

"Dr. Jeff, but where will he go? I can't put him out on the street."

Those were the words I heard in a parent coaching session last week. Let's elaborate with a few fictional examples:

"Ava," 27, has been living with her parents after losing several jobs. When they discuss a timeline to move forward toward greater independence, her mother immediately imagines Ava sleeping in her car.

Then there's Joe, who is behind on his rent again. His dad, Sal, has covered it three times this year. Each time Sal decides this will be the last, the same thing stops him: "I can't let my son become homeless."

Now, let's look at Tammi, who lives at home, contributes very little, and becomes furious when her mother brings up work or any significant responsibilities, for that matter. Stacy, Tammi's mom, wants things to change, but asking Tammi to leave feels unthinkable to her.

I don't think these parents are a bit foolish, but they are a lot scared. In fact, this fear of homelessness can become one of the most powerful forces keeping parents stuck in rescuing.

When Helping Becomes the Only Option

Most parents understandably don't want their adult child sleeping in their car, staying at a shelter, couch surfing, or wondering where they will spend the night. So they help by paying another month's rent, or they cover that overdue electric bill. Or they really cave and allow the adult child to move home with no expectations, or expectations that are said with a hollow ring. Yes, sometimes, plain and simple, that assistance is exactly what the adult child needs. And, yes, a temporary safety net can provide a little breathing room after a job loss, breakup, illness, or setback.

The problems begin when the parent's fear makes continued rescuing feel like the only acceptable choice. This is usually driven by parents getting into catastrophic thinking, such as "If I don't pay this bill, he'll lose his apartment," or "If I don't give her the money, she will end up homeless." Yes, these bad outcomes could come to pass, but when paying the bill no longer feels like a choice and instead feels like an obligation—fueled by the adult child's sense of entitlement, which often has underlying shame—we are no longer in emotionally healthy territory.

When Parents Get Caught in the Rescue Trap

My recent book, The Rescue Trap: How Well-Meaning Parents Keep Their Adult Children Stuck, explains that parents caught in this trap aren't weak or incapable of setting limits. The reason they get caught is that their anxiety gets the best of them as they vividly imagine what might happen if they don't step in. Let's be clear one more time: I am not against helping struggling adult children. But preventing every painful consequence can have messy, unintended effects. Specifically, the adult child may have fewer reasons to tolerate discomfort, solve problems, accept less-than-ideal housing (This is a huge one, by the way!), seek available assistance, or make other difficult changes.

article continues after advertisement

Yes, Compassion and Boundaries Can Coexist

There is no doubt that there are situations such as genuine housing insecurity, mental health issues, economic hardship, and active addictions that can make your adult child's road to independence feel more complicated. But as a parent, ask yourself: "Am I helping my child move forward with some accountability, or am I mainly preventing myself from feeling the anxiety of watching them struggle?" Sometimes the answer may be more uncomfortable than you want to hear. The goal is neither to care less nor carry them more at the cost of understanding (and experiencing) a healthy relationship with the value of the dollar.

As a parent, don't confuse being a safety net with your adult child being unaware that they still have a role to play in their own safety system.

item.title: Two Exercises to Strengthen Your Relationship
item.description:
Relationships

Two Exercises to Strengthen Your Relationship

Reflect on what you give, what you need, and why both matter.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Self-scrutiny can make you more generous to your partner.
  • A partner can't meet your needs if you don't make them known.
  • Humility can be the secret sauce in a relationship.

In my early 20s, I developed a theory about relationships, identifying them as primarily either wide or deep.

Deep relationships, I believed, were rooted in mutual interests and similar life experiences, offering instant compatibility and an alignment that swiftly transcends small talk. They anchor two people in the comfort of feeling deeply known. Grounded in shared passions and often common experiences, they prompt the exclamation, “What?! You too?!”

Wide relationships, by contrast, unite people with different life experiences, backgrounds, and perspectives. They are fueled by curiosity about the differences and the delight of discovery. They jettison us out of our comfort zones, sparking new ideas and adventures. They prompt the exclamation, “Wow, tell me more!”

Neither is inherently better than the other. Most relationships embody elements of both width and depth, though one generally predominates. What matters is which feels like the better fit: cracking out of your comfort zone or relishing deep familiarity.

Not long after I developed my theory, I had to test it. The wide relationship I was in was fast moving toward marriage. How did I know if it was a long-term fit, whether my extremely wide relationship with someone from a different culture and background could go the distance?

I began to grapple with a question every couple must eventually confront, regardless of whether their relationship is primarily wide or deep: Were the things that made us interesting to each other enough for the long haul, or would those very differences eventually undermine us?

As I grappled with a decision, my mother intervened by offering me a book, How to Stop Looking for Someone Perfect and Find Love by Judith Sills, Ph.D.

Assessment of Our Own Desirability

Decades have passed since my then-boyfriend and I read the book and worked our way through the many exercises, but one was particularly helpful and has stayed with me. We were assigned to separately make a list of 10 things that made each of us desirable as a mate, followed by 10 things that made each of us undesirable.

When you are young and confident, the desirable qualities flow easily, and it is generally easy to assess the strengths and shortcomings of a partner. But then we both had to confront the harder question: What would make us difficult to live with?

The exercise altered how we evaluated each other. Rather than asking if the other person met our idealized version of a mate, we were being asked to look at ourselves with equal scrutiny and acknowledge our own imperfections. The reframing enabled us to see two whole people, each an imperfect package, each with qualities another might cherish but also with qualities that would require patience and compromise.

Whether deep or wide, I came to realize that every relationship has fault lines. The exercise suggested what matters most is not how alike or different two people are, but whether each can see the other clearly and accept that strengths and flaws come bundled together.

This exercise illuminated what psychologists have long told us. For a long-term relationship to succeed, we must turn the lens on ourselves. In fact, research suggests that acknowledging and accepting our own imperfections is associated with greater acceptance of our partner's imperfections. When we can see where we may fall short, we tend to be more generous toward the shortcomings of those we love. At its core, this understanding exemplifies the enduring virtue of humility.

I was learning that humility can be the secret sauce in a relationship. Research confirms that humility makes us more appealing at the onset of a relationship and more forgiving once a relationship is established. Prospective partners rated humble individuals favorably and viewed them as more attractive than those who came across as overly confident or even arrogant.

But humility, of course, is important but not the whole of it.

Needs List Exercise

It was decades later that my husband and I were introduced to another exercise: Each of us was assigned to make a list of 10 things we wanted from the other. What fun, I thought! But one look at his face suggested he had reached a far different conclusion.

In a flash, I completed the exercise. My 10-point list amounted to something I later joked was a request that he earn a Ph.D. in our relationship: talk more, express more, plumb the emotional depths.

He took considerably longer with his list and never got to 10. His list, as I recall, stopped at two:

  1. Once in a while, feed the dog.
  2. Turn off the lights when you leave a room.

We laughed about it for years, but the exercise exposed something important. I wanted deeper emotional expression. He wanted a lower electric bill. Both needs were legitimate. What mattered most was that we each respond to what the other wanted.

Relationship scholars call this perceived partner responsiveness, the sense that we are understood, appreciated, and cared for by the person we love. This shared understanding is essential to everyday intimacy. In other words, intimacy is dependent on both partners expressing what they most need and feeling the person they love hears, understands, and responds. Good communication is essential because no one can respond to a need that has not been made visible.

Together, these two exercises point to a deceptively simple truth. Long-term relationships require both humility and responsiveness—enough humility to recognize that you are both imperfect and enough openness to make your needs known while keeping your partner’s needs in view. Sometimes this may require excavating your emotions while also remembering to feed the dog.

After all, there’s no final exam in marriage, just a series of pop quizzes, with the answers changing, as we do.
